questions.q: Binary-search debugging (including git bisect) needs one property of the history. Which?
questions.explain: Binary search throws away half the suspects on each check, which is only valid when "bad" does not come and go. A flaky check or a bug that appears and disappears breaks that, so make the check reliable first.
options: Every commit must have a test
Once the bug appears, every later version is also bad, and the check says good or bad reliably
The history must have a power-of-two number of commits
The bug must throw an error

questions.q: About how many times does git bisect run execute your test on a history of 1,000 commits between good and bad?
questions.explain: Each run halves the range: 1000 → 500 → 250 → … → 1 takes about log₂ 1000 ≈ 10 steps. A million commits would take about 20.

questions.q: During git bisect run, what does it mean when your check script exits with code 125?
questions.explain: Exit 0 is good and 1 to 127 is bad, except 125, which tells bisect to skip the commit. Use it for commits that do not build or start for unrelated reasons.
options: This commit cannot be tested; skip it

questions.q: Why should the check script for git bisect run be untracked (or outside the repository)?
questions.explain: You want the same check at every commit. Old commits may predate the script or contain an older version of it.
options: Git refuses to run tracked files
Bisect checks out old commits; a tracked script could be missing or different there, while untracked files stay unchanged
So that it is not pushed to GitHub by accident

questions.q: What does git bisect reset do?
questions.explain: During bisect, your folder holds whichever old commit was being tested. reset returns you to where you were; it changes nothing in the history.
options: Ends the bisect session and puts your folder back on the branch you started from

questions.q: On some old commits your check crashes with "Cannot find module './invoice.js'" because the file had another name back then. What happens if the script exits 1 there?
questions.explain: Bisect only sees the exit code. A check must fail only for the bug it tests; for "cannot test this commit", exit 125 so it is skipped.
options: Bisect counts those commits as bad and may name the rename as the first bad commit

questions.q: Before starting bisect, why run the check on the commit you plan to mark good?
questions.explain: "It worked last week" is a memory, not evidence. Bisect trusts your good and bad markers completely, so verify them.
options: If it fails there too, the bug is older than you think and bisect would give a meaningless answer

questions.q: In a five-whys analysis, which answer to "Why did the refactor remove the cancelled check?" leads to a useful action?
questions.explain: Blaming a person is a dead end: the next person in the same situation would make the same mistake. The useful answer names something in the situation you can change: give the rule a name and a test.
options: "Because the rule was an unnamed continue with no test, so nothing showed that a business rule was being deleted."

questions.q: When should you stop asking "why?"
questions.explain: "Because floating point is inexact" is true but not actionable; "because we store money as naira floats" is. Five is a guideline, not a rule.
options: When you reach a law of physics or of JavaScript
When the answer is something you can change (code, a test, a process), which gives you an action

questions.q: For the invoice bug, which action works at the level of the root cause rather than the symptom or the direct cause?
questions.explain: Reissuing fixes the symptom; restoring the check fixes this bug; the checklist stops the same kind of bug for other rules. A good analysis produces actions at all three levels.
options: Add "new business rule? add a test" to the pull request checklist
Tell the accountant to check every invoice by hand

questions.q: Why does items.slice(start, start + pageSize - 1) lose an item on every page?
questions.explain: Mixing an inclusive end (how people count) with an exclusive one (how slice works) is the classic off-by-one. The end for slice is simply start + pageSize.
options: slice already excludes its end index, so subtracting 1 removes the last slot a second time

questions.q: 23 orders, 5 per page. Which expression gives the right number of pages?
questions.explain: Four full pages and one partial page make 5. floor gives 4 and hides the last three orders; round happens to work for 23 but fails for 21 (it gives 4).

questions.q: What makes the pagination verification in the lesson stronger than three hand-picked test cases?
questions.explain: A property checked over many generated inputs covers boundaries you might not think of: empty lists, exact multiples, one item. This is property-based testing.
options: It checks a rule ("every item exactly once, in order") for every list length from 0 to 30 and page sizes 1 to 7, including the edge cases

questions.q: Why did the lost-update deposit bug never show up on the developer's laptop?
questions.explain: The race window is the time between reading and writing the balance. Network latency in production makes it wide; locally it is tiny. Reproduce races by controlling the timing, as the lesson's fake database does.
options: The local database answers almost instantly, so two deposits almost never overlap between the read and the write
The bug only exists in TypeScript

questions.q: A race condition disappears as soon as you add console.log calls. What is this called, and what is the better approach?
questions.explain: Logging takes time and shifts when things run. A reproduction that fixes the timing (deliberate delays, a controlled order) shows the bug every time, with or without logs.
options: A syntax error; remove the logs
A heisenbug: observing changes the timing. Reproduce with controlled delays instead of relying on chance
A memory leak; restart the server

questions.q: The shop runs four server processes behind a load balancer. Which fix for lost deposits works across all of them?
questions.explain: An in-memory lock only serialises deposits inside one process. The database is the one place all processes share, and a single atomic statement cannot be interleaved.
options: An in-memory lock per account in each process
An atomic update in the database: UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance + $1 WHERE id = $2

questions.q: Why does the race fix get verified with 20 overlapping deposits, when the report only had 2?
questions.explain: Verification should try hard to break the fix. Races are about probability, so test under more pressure than the original report.
options: A fix that only survives the reported case may just have made the race window smaller; heavy concurrency shows whether it is really gone

questions.q: Inside a method, an error says Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'sent'), and the line is this.sent.push(...). What is the first hypothesis?
questions.explain: The message says the thing before .sent was undefined, and that thing is this. In class code (strict mode), a detached method called as a plain function gets this === undefined.
options: this is undefined: the method was called without its object, for example passed as a callback

questions.q: Writing send = (order) => { … } as a class field fixes forEach(mailer.send). What is the cost?
questions.explain: Arrow functions capture this from where they are created, so a class-field arrow is created per instance. For a few objects that does not matter; for millions it costs memory.
options: The method can no longer use this
Each object gets its own copy of the function instead of sharing one on the prototype

questions.q: 111 * 0.075 prints 8.325, yet Math.round(111 * 0.075 * 100) gives 832, not 833. Why?
questions.explain: 0.075 has no exact binary form, so the product is 8.32499999999999928…. It is displayed as 8.325, but ×100 gives 832.4999999999999, which rounds down. Printing with toPrecision(20) shows the truth.
options: JavaScript prints the shortest decimal that identifies the number; the stored value is slightly below 8.325
0.075 is stored exactly, but 111 is not

questions.q: In the VAT hunt, why compare against a BigInt implementation?
questions.explain: To measure a bug across 100,000 inputs you need an oracle you trust. Exact integer arithmetic has no rounding errors to hide behind.
options: BigInt arithmetic on whole kobo is exact, so it is a trustworthy reference to measure how many prices the float code gets wrong
BigInt is required for VAT by law

questions.q: Why did Bola's new cart contain Ada's rice but not Ada's coupon code?
questions.explain: { ...EMPTY_CART } is a shallow copy. Every cart pointed at the template's array, so push changed it for everyone. Assignment only changes one object's own property.
options: Spread copies property values; items is a reference to one shared array that Ada mutated, while couponCode was replaced on Ada's own object
The cart was saved in a cookie
Arrays are copied deeply but strings are not

questions.q: The shared-cart bug seemed to vanish after every deploy and return later. Why?
questions.explain: Module-level objects are created once per process. State that leaks into them persists until the process restarts, which makes such bugs look intermittent.
options: The template object lives as long as the server process; a restart creates a fresh, empty template until the first customer mutates it again
The bug only happens at night

questions.q: What does deep-freezing EMPTY_CART add, beyond cloning it in newCart?
questions.explain: Cloning fixes today's code. Freezing guards against the whole class of bug: a mutation of the shared object now fails loudly where it happens.
options: Any future code that forgets to clone gets a TypeError at the exact line that mutates the template, instead of silently leaking data
It deletes the template after use

questions.q: Why does order.getDate() give 25 on a laptop in Lagos and 24 on the server for the same order at 2026-09-24T23:30:00Z?
questions.explain: The moment is the same; the local calendar date differs by time zone. Decide which zone a business day belongs to, and compute in it explicitly.
options: getDate uses the local time zone of the machine running the code, and servers usually run in UTC
Dates are stored differently on servers
The laptop's Node.js version is newer

questions.q: An import of ./Invoice.js works on a Mac and fails on the Linux server, where the file is called invoice.js. Why?
questions.explain: An operating-system difference, not a code difference. Running tests in CI on Linux catches it before deployment.
options: Linux does not support ES modules
macOS file systems ignore letter case by default; Linux treats Invoice.js and invoice.js as different files
The server has an older Node.js
The file is corrupted on upload

questions.q: Why is continuous integration (CI) the standard cure for "works on my machine"?
questions.explain: A clean environment has no leftover files, local settings or cached data. If the tests pass there, you know they do not depend on your machine.
options: It runs the tests on every push in a clean, known environment, so they must pass somewhere other than your laptop

questions.q: Which item does not belong in a bug write-up?
questions.explain: Write-ups are blameless: they describe what in the situation let the bug through and what changes prevent it. Blame discourages honest reports.
options: Impact: who was affected and how much
The name of the person to blame

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Eight commits need log₂ 8 = 3 checks: middle 3 (d4, good), then 5 (f6, bad), then 4 (e5, bad). good is 3 and bad is 4, neighbours, so e5 is the first bad commit.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Page 1 is slice(0, 2) and page 2 is slice(3, 5). Order 1003 (and 1006) is never on any page: the last slot of every page is lost.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: floor and ceil agree on exact multiples (0, 20) and differ as soon as there is a partial page. That is why the bug hides when the test data has exactly 20 orders.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: All three deposits read 0 before any of them writes. They then write 0 + 500000, 0 + 200000 and 0 + 100000 in order, and the last write wins. Two deposits are lost.

questions.q: The same deposits, now chained per account. What does this print?
questions.explain: Each deposit starts only after the previous one has finished, so each reads the balance the previous one wrote: 0 → 500000 → 700000 → 800000.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first add is a method call (count 1). forEach(counter.add) calls the detached function with this === undefined and throws on the first item. The bound version adds 2 more: 3.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The float version computes 832.4999999999999 before rounding and goes down. The integer version computes (832500 + 500) / 1000 = 833 exactly: round half up in whole numbers.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Spread is shallow: a.tags, b.tags and DEFAULTS.tags are one array, so the push shows everywhere. priority was replaced on a only.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: structuredClone copies every level, so each object gets its own array and the defaults stay untouched.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The spread copied the reference to the frozen array, and pushing into a frozen array throws. The mutation that would have leaked data now fails at the exact line, which is the point of freezing templates.
options:
TypeError: Cannot add property 0, object is not extensible
0

TypeError: Cannot assign to read only property 'items'
0

questions.q: These use only UTC-based methods, so the output is the same on every machine. What does it print?
questions.explain: 00:30 in Lagos (UTC+1) is 23:30 UTC on the previous day, so the UTC date is 24. A date-only string like "2026-09-25" is parsed as midnight UTC.

questions.q: Write firstBad(builds, isBad): given builds in order, where every build from some point on is bad, return the first bad one using binary search. Also count and return how many times isBad was called.
questions.explain: The invariant: good is known good, bad is known bad. Each check moves one of them to the middle, halving the gap, so 64 builds need 6 checks. This is exactly what git bisect does with commits.

questions.q: Write a correct paginate(items, page, pageSize) returning { items, totalPages } with 1-based pages. Walking all pages of 23 orders at 5 per page must show all 23.
questions.explain: slice's end is exclusive, so the end is start + pageSize. Page counts round up with Math.ceil so the partial last page exists.

questions.q: Write withLock(key, task) so that tasks with the same key run one after another (even if one fails), while different keys may overlap. The deposits must not be lost.
questions.explain: Each task is chained onto the previous promise for its key, so it starts only when the previous one has settled. then(task, task) runs it after a failure too, and storing next.catch(() => {}) keeps one failure from rejecting every later task.

questions.q: The mailer throws when its method is passed as a callback. Fix it in the constructor by binding send, without changing the call sites.
questions.explain: this.send.bind(this) creates a function whose this is fixed to the object, and stores it as an own property, which shadows the prototype method. Detached calls now work.

questions.q: Write vatKobo(priceKobo) for 7.5% VAT, rounding half a kobo up, using only integer arithmetic. It must throw for a price that is not a non-negative safe integer.
questions.explain: 7.5% is 75/1000. Multiplying first keeps everything an exact integer; adding half the divisor (500) before flooring rounds half up. ₦3.00 → 22.5 kobo → 23, which the float version got wrong.
questions.expected:
833 750 23
price must be whole kobo, got 111.5

questions.q: Fix newCart so every cart gets its own items array. Ada's rice must not appear in Bola's cart.
questions.explain: structuredClone copies the nested array, so each cart owns its items and the template stays empty. Writing the literal { items: [], couponCode: null, owner } in the function works just as well.

questions.q: Write deepFreeze(value) that freezes an object and every object or array inside it, at any depth, and returns it.
questions.explain: Object.freeze is shallow, so recurse into every object value first (arrays included, since Object.values works on them). Frozen templates turn silent shared-state bugs into immediate errors.

questions.q: Write dayKey(date, timeZone) that returns the calendar date YYYY-MM-DD in the given time zone, whatever the machine's own zone is. Use Intl.DateTimeFormat with the "en-CA" locale, which formats dates as YYYY-MM-DD.
questions.explain: Passing timeZone explicitly makes the result independent of the server's TZ. The business decides which zone a "day" belongs to (Lagos for a Lagos shop); the code should say so.
